newsitem.title: THAILAND: Amnuay's departure to deepen Thai economic crisis.
newsitem.headline: Amnuay's departure to deepen Thai economic crisis.

text.p: Thai finance minister Amnuay Viravan's resignation will deepen Thailand's economic crisis, and analysts said it was a blow to foreign investor confidence in the country.
Amnuay quit on Thursday over differences with political rivals in Prime Minister Chavalit Yongchaiyudh's six-party coalition government concerning his management of the troubled economy.

His departure after less than seven months in the job raised concerns about the possible dismantling of the fiscal and monetary disciplines he had adopted, which would further erode foreign confidence in Thailand, the analysts said.

"Foreign investors hope the government would stick to his monetary and fiscal disciplines...but this is made uncertain by the fact the Chart Pattana Party is known for its expansionary policies," said Mike Stead of Union Securities Plc.
His resignation also would mean more trouble for the country's frail economy, and currency and stock markets, the analysts told Reuters.
The news triggered a fall on the fragile Thai stock market and offshore selling of the baht on Thursday.

"His timing is not good, coming as our business and financial sectors are struggling to survive. It will produce at least a negative impact here and abroad," said Preecha Jarungidanan of Chao Phaya Finance and Securities Plc.

Amnuay has left behind an economy growing at its slowest pace in more than a decade, a financial sector on the verge of collapse due to over-exposure to property projects, and a Thai baht that has suffered speculative attacks.
Economic growth for 1997 is seen officially at 5.9 percent, against 6.4 percent last year. Economists expect even lower growth of between three and five percent.
The stock market is at an eight-year low, exports have turned sluggish, and investment and spending have slowed.

Graham Catterwell, managing director of Deutsche Morgan Grenfell (Thailand), urged Thailand to seek advice from the International Monetary Fund (IMF) on how to deal with its widening economic problems.

The analysts said Chart Pattana would likely back any move for a relaxation of Thailand's foreign exchange regime. Such a move would involve widening a long-standing four satang currency trading band within which the Bank of Thailand trades the baht with commercial banks.

Chart Pattana is led by former premier Chatichai Choonhavan, chairman of premier Chavalit's advisory council. The party, the second biggest in the ruling coalition, has been at odds with Amnuay over his economic remedies in past months.
Most brokers and analysts had approved of Amnuay's policy initiatives, including steep budget cuts and backing the Bank of Thailand's stout defence of the baht against speculative attacks.
The analysts partly attributed Amnuay's limited success in handling economic problems to his status as a non-elected cabinet member, a position often challenged by rival politicians in the coalition.
"Amnuay has retained his good image, but I am not sure whether his sluggish performance was due to government structural or personnel problems," said Preecha of Chao Phaya.
Analysts said the extent of the economic fallout from Amnuay's resignation would be determined by the speed at which Chavalit names a successor.
"The question is how long will it take to name a successor and how creditable he will be in the eyes of foreigners," a foreign analyst said.

Said Stead of Union Securities: "The situation is very messy. His successor would likely be a non-elected financial expert who would face the same problem of squabbling with Chart Pattana on economic policies."
Analysts said there was no clear successor for Amnuay. They said one outstanding prospective candidate was former finance minister Virabongsa Ramangkura, who was noted for his conservative policies.
Virabongsa was generally regarded as having played a key role in the last Thai baht devaluation in 1984.
One of the first tasks for Amnuay's successor will be to represent the government in a scheduled June 25-27 parliamentary debate on the 1997/1998 (October/September) fiscal budget.
